extracted.intended_audience: EPO examiners, patent attorneys, and practitioners assessing inventive step under the EPC
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying the EPO 'problem‑solution approach' to assess inventive step under Article 56 EPC, including selection of closest prior art, formulation of the objective technical problem, and application of the would/not could test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 56 EPC — Inventive Step (Non-obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 56 EPC requires that an invention, having regard to the state of the art, must not be obvious to a person skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central legal provision governing inventive step; assessment asks whether the claimed invention would have been obvious to a skilled person in view of the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem‑Solution Approach (methodology)
rubrics_metrics.description: The problem and solution approach is used almost universally at the EPO in the examination of inventive step: the obviousness question is broken up into three separate questions (identify closest prior art; determine the objective technical problem; apply the would/could test).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since 1977 the EPO applies this three‑step method as a tool to structure inventive step assessment. It is a methodological framework — not a substitute definition of inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the closest prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Select the single reference disclosing the most similar combination of features and addressing the same purpose as the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closest prior art should: be from the same or closely related technical field; address a similar problem or purpose; have the most relevant technical features in common with the claimed invention; require the minimum modifications to arrive at the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine the objective technical problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulate the 'objective' technical problem in light of the closest prior art; it may differ from the problem identified by the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The objective problem is reformulated based on the technical effects achieved by the distinguishing features and on the closest prior art (not all prior art). When formulating the problem take care to avoid hindsight by avoiding pointers to the solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the would/not could test
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask whether the skilled person would (not could) have arrived at the claimed invention starting from the closest prior art and faced with the objective technical problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Central to EPO (and UPC) practice: obvious inventions are those that the unimaginative skilled person would arrive at. Use 'would' rather than 'could' to prevent hindsight-based justifications that a skilled person might possibly combine or modify disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on use and validity of the problem‑solution approach
rubrics_metrics.description: The problem and solution approach is a tool to be used in assessing inventive step and not a definition that substitutes for the actual requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An argument of lack of inventive step using the problem‑solution approach is only valid if both: (1) the problem is known or is obvious in view of the state of the art; and (2) the solution to the problem is obvious in view of the state of the art. Do not treat the method as automatically decisive without satisfying these conditions.
